claim: Lung squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC) has an incidence of over 600,000 cases per year.
source: Lung squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC) is a considerable global health burden, with an incidence of over 600,000 cases per year.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract providing epidemiological data about LSCC incidence.

claim: LSCC patients have a 5-year survival rate of less than 5%.
source: Treatment options are limited, and patient's 5-year survival rate is less than 5%.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract about patient survival rates.

claim: USP28 stabilizes the oncoproteins c-MYC, c-JUN, and Δp63.
source: The ubiquitin-specific protease 28 (USP28) has been implicated in tumourigenesis through its stabilization of the oncoproteins c-MYC, c-JUN, and Δp63.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information about USP28 function.

claim: Genetic inactivation of Usp28 induced regression of established murine LSCC lung tumours.
source: Here, we show that genetic inactivation of Usp28-induced regression of established murine LSCC lung tumours.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: A small molecule inhibitor of USP28 was developed that inhibits USP28 activity in the low nanomole range.
source: We developed a small molecule that inhibits USP28 activity in the low nanomole range.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by biochemical assay data in Figure 4.

claim: The USP28 inhibitor displays cross-reactivity against USP25.
source: While displaying cross-reactivity against the closest homologue USP25, this inhibitor showed a high degree of selectivity over other deubiquitinases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by activity-based probe profiling data in Figure 4D.

claim: USP28 inhibitor treatment resulted in a dramatic decrease in c-MYC, c-JUN, and Δp63 protein levels.
source: USP28 inhibitor treatment resulted in a dramatic decrease in c-MYC, c-JUN, and Δp63 proteins levels and consequently induced substantial regression of autochthonous murine LSCC tumours and human LSCC xenografts, thereby phenocopying the effect observed by genetic deletion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by Western blot and immunohistochemistry data in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: USP28 inhibitor treatment induced substantial regression of autochthonous murine LSCC tumours.
source: USP28 inhibitor treatment resulted in a dramatic decrease in c-MYC, c-JUN, and Δp63 proteins levels and consequently induced substantial regression of autochthonous murine LSCC tumours and human LSCC xenografts, thereby phenocopying the effect observed by genetic deletion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by histological data in Figure 5.

claim: USP28 inhibitor treatment induced substantial regression of human LSCC xenografts.
source: USP28 inhibitor treatment resulted in a dramatic decrease in c-MYC, c-JUN, and Δp63 proteins levels and consequently induced substantial regression of autochthonous murine LSCC tumours and human LSCC xenografts, thereby phenocopying the effect observed by genetic deletion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by xenograft tumor growth data in Figure 6.

claim: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide.
source: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: No targeted treatment options exist for LSCC patients.
source: However, no targeted treatment options exist for LSCC patients (Hirsch et al., 2017; Novello et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Platinum-based chemotherapy remains the cornerstone of current LSCC treatment despite having limited efficacy on LSCC patient survival.
source: Consequently, despite having limited efficacy on LSCC patient survival, platinum-based chemotherapy remains the cornerstone of current LSCC treatment (Fennell et al., 2016; Isaka et al., 2017; Scagliotti et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: FBW7 is the substrate recognition component of an SCF-type ubiquitin ligase.
source: The Fbxw7 protein product F-box/WD repeat-containing protein 7 (FBW7) is the substrate recognition component of an SCF-type ubiquitin ligase, which targets several well-known oncoproteins, including c-MYC, NOTCH, and c-JUN, for degradation (Davis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: FBW7 targets c-MYC, NOTCH, and c-JUN for degradation.
source: The Fbxw7 protein product F-box/WD repeat-containing protein 7 (FBW7) is the substrate recognition component of an SCF-type ubiquitin ligase, which targets several well-known oncoproteins, including c-MYC, NOTCH, and c-JUN, for degradation (Davis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Genetic analyses of human LSCC samples revealed common genomic alterations in Fbxw7.
source: These oncoproteins accumulate in the absence of FBW7 function, and genetic analyses of human LSCC samples revealed common genomic alterations in Fbxw7 (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012; Kan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: FBW7 protein is undetectable by immunohistochemistry in 69% of LSCC patient tumour samples.
source: In addition, FBW7 protein is undetectable by immunohistochemistry (IHC) in 69% of LSCC patient tumour samples (Ruiz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Genetically engineered mice harbouring loss of Fbxw7 concomitant with KrasG12D activation develop LSCC with 100% penetrance and short latency.
source: Genetically engineered mice (GEM) harbouring loss of Fbxw7 concomitant with KrasG12D activation (KF mice) develop LSCC with 100% penetrance and short latency, as well as LADC (Ruiz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: FBW7 is an important tumour suppressor in both human and murine lung cancer.
source: Thus, FBW7 is an important tumour suppressor in both human and murine lung cancer.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the introduction based on cited evidence.

claim: USP28 opposes FBW7-mediated ubiquitination of c-MYC and c-JUN.
source: The deubiquitinase USP28 opposes FBW7-mediated ubiquitination of the oncoproteins c-MYC and c-JUN, thereby stabilizing these proteins (Popov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Deleting Usp28 in a murine model of colorectal cancer reduced size of established tumours and increased lifespan.
source: In a murine model of colorectal cancer, deleting Usp28 reduced size of established tumours and increased lifespan (Diefenbacher et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: MYC was transcriptionally upregulated in human LSCC compared to healthy lung tissue or LADC tumours.
source: MYC was transcriptionally upregulated in human LSCC compared to healthy lung tissue or LADC tumours (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: qPCR analysis on primary human lung biopsy samples confirmed that MYC is highly expressed in LSCC tumours compared with normal lung tissue.
source: Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis on an independent set of primary human lung biopsy samples confirmed that MYC is highly expressed in LSCC tumours compared with normal lung tissue (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: IHC staining on primary lung tumours confirmed a significant abundance of c-MYC protein in LSCC samples.
source: Moreover, IHC staining on primary lung tumours confirmed a significant abundance of c-MYC protein in LSCC samples (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Δp63 and c-JUN showed higher protein levels in LSCC compared to LADC tumours.
source: Also, Δp63 and c-JUN, critical factors in squamous cell identity and tumour maintenance, respectively, showed higher protein levels in LSCC compared to LADC tumours (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Individual downregulation of c-MYC, c-JUN, and Δp63 by siRNA resulted in a significant reduction of cell growth in four independent human LSCC cell lines.
source: Individual downregulation of c-MYC, c-JUN, and Δp63 by small interfering RNA (siRNA) resulted in a significant reduction of cell growth in four independent human LSCC cell lines (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: 25% of human LSCC cases show gain-of-function alterations in USP28.
source: We observed that 25% of human LSCC cases show gain-of-function alterations in USP28 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A positive correlation between USP28 copy-number and mRNA expression was found in TCGA datasets.
source: In addition, a positive correlation between USP28 copy-number and mRNA expression was found in the same datasets (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Low USP28 mRNA levels correlated with low USP28 protein levels in human LSCC samples.
source: Interestingly, qPCR and IHC analysis on human LSCC samples revealed that low USP28 mRNA levels correlated with low USP28 protein levels and likewise, high/moderate mRNA levels also correlated with high USP28 protein levels (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qPCR and IHC data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Usp28 downregulation by shRNA resulted in a significant reduction in c-MYC, c-JUN, and Δp63 protein levels in LSCC primary tumour cells.
source: Usp28 downregulation by shRNA resulted in a significant reduction in c-MYC, c-JUN, and Δp63 protein levels in LSCC primary tumour cells and reduced LSCC cell growth (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Usp28 downregulation by shRNA reduced LSCC cell growth.
source: Usp28 downregulation by shRNA resulted in a significant reduction in c-MYC, c-JUN, and Δp63 protein levels in LSCC primary tumour cells and reduced LSCC cell growth (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Usp28 was shown to be required for the initiation of lung tumours in the Rosa26-Cas9 sgRNA KrasG12D; Trp53; Lkb1 model.
source: Recently, Usp28 was shown to be required for the initiation of lung tumours in the Rosa26-Cas9 sgRNA KrasG12D; Trp53; Lkb1 model (Prieto-Garcia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation.

claim: Loss of USP28 expression decreased LADC tumour size but did not reduce the number of LADC tumours in KFCU mice.
source: Although the loss of USP28 expression decreased LADC tumour size, it did not reduce the number of LADC tumours (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Histological examination of KFCU mice revealed a clear reduction in the numbers of LSCC lesions in Usp28-deleted lungs.
source: In contrast, histological examination of KFCU mice revealed a clear reduction in the numbers of LSCC lesions in Usp28-deleted lungs (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by histological data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The few CK5-positive LSCC lesions that remained after Usp28 deletion were substantially smaller than control tumours.
source: As well as a significant reduction in tumour number, the few CK5-positive LSCC lesions that remained were substantially smaller than control tumours (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by tumor size measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Measurement of 429 individual KFCU LSCC tumours showed an average size of 11.4 × 10^4 μm^2 in the vehicle arm versus 4.6 × 10^4 μm^2 in the tamoxifen arm.
source: Measurement of the size of 429 individual KFCU LSCC tumours (326 vehicle-treated and 103 tamoxifen-treated) showed an average size of 11.4 × 104 μm2 in the vehicle arm versus 4.6 × 104 μm2 in the tamoxifen arm (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by tumor size measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Usp28 deletion resulted in apoptotic cell death in LSCC tumours.
source: Immunoblotting analysis revealed that Usp28 deletion resulted in apoptotic cell death (cleaved caspase-3; CC3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Usp28 deletion decreased c-JUN and c-MYC protein levels in KFCU LADC lesions.
source: Usp28 deletion also decreased c-JUN and c-MYC levels in KFCU LADC lesions, although the reduction in c-MYC protein levels was significantly less pronounced than observed in LSCC (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Elimination of Usp28 has little effect on apoptotic cell death in LADC lesions.
source: Strikingly, elimination of Usp28 has little effect, if any, on apoptotic cell death, as determined by its inability to induce CC3 in LADC lesions.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Loss of USP28 expression in the KPCU LADC model did not result in a reduction of LADC tumour number and size.
source: Loss of USP28 expression in this second LADC model also did not result in a reduction of LADC tumour number and size (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by histological data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: FT206 interferes with USP28/25 probe labelling in LSCC H520 cell extracts with EC50 ~300–1000 nM.
source: Using this approach, we found that the compound FT206 interferes with USP28/25 probe labelling (USP-ABP versus USP) in LSCC H520 cell extracts (EC50 ~300–1000 nM, Figure 4B) and intact cells (EC50 ~1–3 μM, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by activity-based probe assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: FT206 interferes with USP28/25 probe labelling in intact LSCC H520 cells with EC50 ~1–3 μM.
source: Using this approach, we found that the compound FT206 interferes with USP28/25 probe labelling (USP-ABP versus USP) in LSCC H520 cell extracts (EC50 ~300–1000 nM, Figure 4B) and intact cells (EC50 ~1–3 μM, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by activity-based probe assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: AZ1 appeared to exert lower potency towards USP28 (EC50 >30 μM) and selectivity for USP25 (EC50 ~10–30 μM).
source: In contrast to FT206, AZ1, a different USP28 inhibitor (Wrigley et al., 2017), based on a benzylic amino ethanol scaffold, appeared to exert lower potency towards USP28 (EC50 >30 μM) and selectivity for USP25 (EC50 ~10–30 μM) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by activity-based probe assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Activity-based probe profiling in human LSCC cells revealed a remarkable USP28/25 selectivity for FT206 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: When performing such assay in human LSCC cells, we were able to profile 28 endogenous DUBs, revealing a remarkable USP28/25 selectivity for FT206 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The ubiquitination levels of c-MYC and c-JUN increased upon FT206 and MG132 co-treatment.
source: The ubiquitination levels of c-MYC and c-JUN increased upon FT206 and MG132 co-treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), confirming that FT206 blocks USP28-mediated deubiquitination of its substrates.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TUBE pulldown data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The ubiquitination level of USP28 increased upon FT206 treatment.
source: The ubiquitination level of USP28 also increased upon FT206 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which is consistent with previous observations where the enzymatic activity of DUBs can function to enhance their own stability (de Bie and Ciechanover, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TUBE pulldown data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment of LSCC tumour cells with FT206 resulted in reduced c-MYC, c-JUN, Δp63, and USP28 protein levels, which were restored upon addition of MG132.
source: Consequently, treatment of LSCC tumour cells with FT206 resulted in reduced c-MYC, c-JUN, Δp63, and USP28 protein levels, which were restored upon addition of MG132 (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FT206 treatment impaired LSCC cell growth.
source: Finally, FT206 treatment impaired LSCC cell growth (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In a USP28-depleted background, FT206 neither affected cell growth nor reduced c-MYC protein levels.
source: However, in a USP28-depleted background, FT206 neither affected cell growth nor reduced c-MYC protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by cell proliferation and Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: FT206 administration at 75 mg/kg three times a week for 5 weeks had no noticeable adverse effects and treated mice maintained normal body weight.
source: FT206 administration had no noticeable adverse effects and treated mice maintained normal body weight (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by body weight monitoring data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The number of KF LADC lesions was not affected by USP28 inhibition via FT206 treatment.
source: Consistent with the effects observed by genetic Usp28 inactivation (Figure 2C), the number of KF LADC lesions was not affected by USP28 inhibition via FT206 treatment (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by histological data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: FT206 effectively reduced LSCC tumour number by 68% (31–10 LSCC tumours).
source: By contrast, we found that FT206 effectively reduced LSCC tumour number by 68% (31–10 LSCC tumours, Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by histological data shown in Figure 5B and E.

claim: Measurement of 252 individual KF LSCC mutant tumours showed a significant reduction of over 45% in tumour size upon FT206 treatment: an average of 8.5 × 10^4 μm^2 in the vehicle arm versus 4.5 × 10^4 μm^2 in the FT206 cohort.
source: Moreover, measurement of 252 individual KF LSCC mutant tumours (156 vehicle-treated and 96 FT206-treated lesions) showed a significant reduction of over 45% in tumour size upon FT206 treatment: an average of 8.5 × 104 μm2 in the vehicle arm versus 4.5 × 104 μm2 in the FT206 cohort (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by tumor size measurements shown in Figure 5F.

claim: USP28 inhibition by FT206 leads to a reduction of total LSCC burden of over 85% by single agent treatment.
source: Thus, USP28 inhibition by FT206 leads to a dramatic reduction in the numbers of advanced LSCC tumours, and the small number of remaining LSCC lesions is significantly reduced in size, resulting in a reduction of total LSCC burden of over 85% by single agent treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is calculated from the tumor number and size data.

claim: Treatment of KF mice with FT206 resulted in reduced Δp63, c-JUN, and c-MYC protein levels.
source: In line with the effects found by genetic Usp28 deletion, treatment of KF mice with FT206 also resulted in reduced Δp63, c-JUN, and c-MYC protein levels (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by IHC data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: FT206 treatment led to a substantial increase in the number of CC3-positive cells in LSCC while LADC cells were not significantly affected.
source: Consequently, FT206 treatment led to a substantial increase in the number of CC3-positive cells in LSCC while LADC cells were not significantly affected, indicating that USP28 inhibition causes apoptotic cell death of LSCC tumour cells (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by IHC data shown in Figure 5H and I.

claim: In KFCU mice pre-exposed to tamoxifen to delete Usp28, USP28 inhibition by FT206 did not result in either a further reduction of LADC and LSCC lesions or body weight loss.
source: Finally, to further confirm the specificity of FT206, KFCU mice pre-exposed to tamoxifen to delete the conditional Usp28 floxed alleles were further treated with the USP28 inhibitor FT206. In this setting, USP28 inhibition did not result in either a further reduction of LADC and LSCC lesions or body weight loss (Figure 2C and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that FT206 targets specifically USP28.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by histological and body weight data shown in Figure 2C, F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: siRNA-mediated USP28 depletion considerably reduced protein levels of Δp63, c-JUN, and c-MYC and impaired growth in human LSCC tumour cells.
source: siRNA-mediated USP28 but not USP25 depletion, and USP28 inhibitor treatment, considerably reduced protein levels of Δp63, c-JUN, and c-MYC and impaired growth in human LSCC tumour cells (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot and cell proliferation data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: USP28 inhibitor treatment considerably reduced protein levels of Δp63, c-JUN, and c-MYC and impaired growth in human LSCC tumour cells.
source: siRNA-mediated USP28 but not USP25 depletion, and USP28 inhibitor treatment, considerably reduced protein levels of Δp63, c-JUN, and c-MYC and impaired growth in human LSCC tumour cells (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot and cell proliferation data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: FT206 treatment had marginal effects on c-MYC and c-JUN protein levels in human LADC cells.
source: In contrast, FT206 treatment had marginal effects on c-MYC and c-JUN protein levels in human LADC cells and in USP28 mutant LSCC cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: FT206 treatment had marginal effects on c-MYC and c-JUN protein levels in USP28 mutant LSCC cells.
source: In contrast, FT206 treatment had marginal effects on c-MYC and c-JUN protein levels in human LADC cells and in USP28 mutant LSCC cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: FT206 led to a remarkable growth impairment of xenografts derived from three independent human LSCC cell lines.
source: Crucially, FT206 led to a remarkable growth impairment of xenografts derived from three independent human LSCC cell lines (Figure 6D–I), which was accompanied with a strong reduction of c-MYC protein levels (Figure 6J–L).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 6D-I.

claim: FT206 treatment of human LSCC xenografts was accompanied with a strong reduction of c-MYC protein levels.
source: Crucially, FT206 led to a remarkable growth impairment of xenografts derived from three independent human LSCC cell lines (Figure 6D–I), which was accompanied with a strong reduction of c-MYC protein levels (Figure 6J–L).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by IHC data shown in Figure 6J-L.

claim: Mice lacking Usp28 are healthy.
source: Importantly, mice lacking Usp28 are healthy (Knobel et al., 2014), suggesting that USP28 is dispensable for normal physiology and homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: USP28 is dispensable for normal physiology and homeostasis.
source: Importantly, mice lacking Usp28 are healthy (Knobel et al., 2014), suggesting that USP28 is dispensable for normal physiology and homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from cited evidence.

claim: USP28 small-molecule inhibition phenocopies the effects of Usp28 deletion in LSCC regression.
source: USP28 small-molecule inhibition phenocopies the effects of Usp28 deletion in LSCC regression, consistent with on-target activity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: TP63, c-JUN, and c-MYC protein levels are increased in LSCC compared to LADC.
source: TP63, c-JUN, and c-MYC protein levels are increased in LSCC compared to LADC (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The frequent downregulation of FBXW7 in human LSCC may underlie the increased accumulation of SCF(Fbw7) substrate proteins like c-MYC, c-JUN, and ΔP63 in LSCC.
source: The frequent downregulation of FBXW7 in human LSCC (Ruiz et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) may underlie the increased accumulation of SCF(Fbw7) substrate proteins like c-MYC, c-JUN, and ΔP63 in LSCC, and thereby cause LSCC tumours to be increasingly dependent on USP28 function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis based on cited evidence and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: All human LSCC cell lines used in the xenograft experiment do not show gain- or loss-of-function mutations in USP28 nor FBXW7.
source: Interestingly, all human LSCC cell lines used in the xenograft experiment (Figure 6), each of which responded well to USP28 inhibition, do not show neither gain- or loss-of-function mutations in USP28 nor FBXW7, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an observation about the cell lines used.

claim: USP28 inhibition might be a therapeutic option for many LSCC patients regardless of USP28/FBXW7 mutation status.
source: Thus, these data support the notion that LSCC tumour cells respond to USP28 inhibition, regardless of USP28/FBXW7 mutation status, which suggest that USP28 inhibition might be a therapeutic option for many LSCC patients.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion based on the xenograft data.

claim: USP28 is a key mediator of LSCC maintenance and progression.
source: In summary, our studies demonstrate that USP28 is a key mediator of LSCC maintenance and progression and hence USP28 represents an exciting therapeutic target.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: USP28 represents an exciting therapeutic target for LSCC.
source: In summary, our studies demonstrate that USP28 is a key mediator of LSCC maintenance and progression and hence USP28 represents an exciting therapeutic target.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: USP28 inhibition should be considered as a potential therapy for human LSCC.
source: Therefore, USP28 inhibition should be considered as a potential therapy for human LSCC.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: FT206 preferentially inhibits USP28 compared to USP25.
source: FT206, the compound used in this study, preferentially inhibits USP28 compared to USP25, whereas AZ1, the compound used by Prieto-Garcia et al., showed a pronounced activity towards USP25.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a comparison between different inhibitors.

claim: FT206 inhibits USP28 in the nano-molar range.
source: In addition, FT206 inhibits USP28 in the nano-molar range, while Prieto-Garcia et al. typically used AZ1 at 10–30 μM, possibly because higher compound concentrations are required for therapeutic inhibition of USP28.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the EC50 data in Figure 4.

claim: Δp63 and c-JUN are critical factors in squamous cell identity and tumour maintenance, respectively.
source: Also, Δp63 and c-JUN, critical factors in squamous cell identity and tumour maintenance, respectively, showed higher protein levels in LSCC compared to LADC tumours (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results as background knowledge about these proteins.

claim: Higher expression of USP28 is associated with a significantly shorter survival time.
source: Since USP28 is involved in Δp63, c-JUN, and c-MYC stabilization and higher expression of USP28 is associated with a significantly shorter survival time (Prieto-Garcia et al., 2020), we targeted its expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation.

claim: c-MYC is a transcription factor that orchestrates a potent pro-cancer programme across multiple cellular pathways.
source: c-MYC is a transcription factor that orchestrates a potent pro-cancer programme across multiple cellular pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge about c-MYC.

claim: c-MYC is often overexpressed in late-stage cancer.
source: As c-MYC is often overexpressed in late-stage cancer, targeting it for degradation is an attractive strategy in many settings.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge.

claim: The deubiquitylase family of enzymes have emerged as attractive drug targets.
source: The deubiquitylase family of enzymes have emerged as attractive drug targets, which can offer a means to destabilize client proteins that might otherwise be undruggable (Schauer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Usp28 inactivation significantly reduces both the number and the size of LSCC tumours.
source: Thus, Usp28 inactivation significantly reduces both the number and the size of LSCC tumours.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the tumor measurement data.

claim: USP28 and its substrates are required for the maintenance of LSCC tumours.
source: Thus, these data suggest that USP28 and its substrates are required for the maintenance of LSCC tumours.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The effects of FT206 are mediated by USP28.
source: Thus, this data suggests that the effects of FT206 are mediated by USP28.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the USP28 depletion experiment with FT206 treatment.

claim: FT206 blocks USP28-mediated deubiquitination of its substrates.
source: The ubiquitination levels of c-MYC and c-JUN increased upon FT206 and MG132 co-treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), confirming that FT206 blocks USP28-mediated deubiquitination of its substrates.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the TUBE pulldown data.

claim: USP28 inhibition causes apoptotic cell death of LSCC tumour cells.
source: Consequently, FT206 treatment led to a substantial increase in the number of CC3-positive cells in LSCC while LADC cells were not significantly affected, indicating that USP28 inhibition causes apoptotic cell death of LSCC tumour cells (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the cleaved caspase-3 staining data.

claim: FT206 targets specifically USP28.
source: Finally, to further confirm the specificity of FT206, KFCU mice pre-exposed to tamoxifen to delete the conditional Usp28 floxed alleles were further treated with the USP28 inhibitor FT206. In this setting, USP28 inhibition did not result in either a further reduction of LADC and LSCC lesions or body weight loss (Figure 2C and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that FT206 targets specifically USP28.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the genetic deletion plus inhibitor treatment experiment.

claim: LSCC tumour cells respond to USP28 inhibition, regardless of USP28/FBXW7 mutation status.
source: Thus, these data support the notion that LSCC tumour cells respond to USP28 inhibition, regardless of USP28/FBXW7 mutation status, which suggest that USP28 inhibition might be a therapeutic option for many LSCC patients.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the xenograft data.

claim: Differences in the selectivity and potency of USP28 inhibitor compounds may explain some of the differences observed between studies.
source: Therefore, differences in the selectivity and potency of the compounds used may explain some of the differences observed.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis to explain differences with another study.

claim: LSCC tumours to be increasingly dependent on USP28 function due to increased accumulation of SCF(Fbw7) substrate proteins.
source: The frequent downregulation of FBXW7 in human LSCC (Ruiz et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) may underlie the increased accumulation of SCF(Fbw7) substrate proteins like c-MYC, c-JUN, and ΔP63 in LSCC, and thereby cause LSCC tumours to be increasingly dependent on USP28 function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis based on the data.

claim: The enzymatic activity of DUBs can function to enhance their own stability.
source: The ubiquitination level of USP28 also increased upon FT206 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which is consistent with previous observations where the enzymatic activity of DUBs can function to enhance their own stability (de Bie and Ciechanover, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation.

claim: Usp28 deficiency corrected the accumulation of SCF (Fbw7) substrate proteins, including c-JUN and c-MYC, in Fbw7 mutant cells.
source: We previously found that Usp28 deficiency corrected the accumulation of SCF (Fbw7) substrate proteins, including c-JUN and c-MYC, in Fbw7 mutant cells (Diefenbacher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Δp63, c-JUN, and c-MYC are all relevant targets of USP28 in LSCC.
source: Indeed, our study suggests that those three oncoproteins are all relevant targets of USP28 in LSCC (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the Western blot data shown in Figure 2H.
